item.title: Inverse Reconstruction of Double Imaging Schlieren
item.description: arXiv:2610.33214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Double imaging is a common artefact in off-axis single-mirror Schlieren systems. Depending on the distance between the object of interest and the mirror, together with the off-axis imaging geometry, such systems often capture images containing a superposition of the target image and a displaced ghost image, resulting in the so-called double imaging phenomenon. This not only degrades image quality, but also complicates its interpretation. To address this problem, we present a new model for ghost image displacement that takes into consideration finite-aperture support, defocus, and magnification. We then use this model to reconstruct the target image via total variation regularisation with a matrix-free alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Extensive experiments using both synthetic and real Schlieren images validate the proposed model, show the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm, and evaluate its performance under parameter mismatch. The proposed framework provides a computational alternative to hardware-based suppression of double imaging, enabling physics-consistent reconstruction while preserving the simplicity and compactness of off-axis single-mirror Schlieren systems.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Saxena, Jo\~ao F. C. Mota

item.title: Contact-Free Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Mechanophenotyping by Amplitude-Modulated Ultrasound and Phase-Locked Optical Diffraction Tomography: Computational Feasibility and Initial Experimental Readouts
item.description: arXiv:2610.33369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether acoustic stimulation combined with phase-locked optical diffraction tomography (ODT) could measure the mechanical responses of the nucleus and cytoplasm separately in adherent cells. A megahertz ultrasound carrier is amplitude-modulated at low frequencies, while angle-scanned holography provides a route to reconstruct the first-harmonic refractive-index response in three dimensions. We built a computational model connecting viscoelastic finite-element simulations of MDA-MB-231 cells with a refractive-index phantom, hologram formation, camera noise and ODT reconstruction. Under an assumed 0.1 Pa harmonic shear traction at 10 Hz, the model predicts 3.6 to 9.2 nm of nuclear shear and 6.6 to 15.1 nm of apical motion. The nuclear-to-cytoplasmic amplitude ratio (R_A) is primarily sensitive to stiffness contrast in the tested scenarios, while the relative phase (Delta phi) responds to differences in dissipation. A simulated protocol using 100 illumination angles and 16 phase visits per angle recovered an imposed stiffening and recovery trajectory after averaging four acquisitions. We also obtained initial 3D tomograms of adherent MDA-MB-231 cells and report preliminary regional measurements from five cells. Their mean amplitude ratio was 0.616 plus or minus 0.098, and their mean relative phase was -1.91 plus or minus 0.58 degrees (mean and between-cell sample standard deviation). All five amplitude ratios were below unity, and all phase differences were negative, consistent with the qualitative directions of selected model scenarios. The small cohort and the absence of independently quantified experimental phase noise prevent a claim of quantitative mechanical validation. Together, these results support further evaluation of phase-locked acoustic ODT and identify experimental requirements for a controlled validation study.
item.dc:creator: Yagmur Isik, Merve Sevgi, Esmahan Caglar, Aysenur Akgun, Hasan Berkay Abdioglu, Gokhan Bora Esmer, Huseyin Uvet

item.title: Polarization-resolved haze in transparent wood - towards wooden glass
item.description: arXiv:2610.33459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transparent wood (TW) composites possess residual haze that limits image clarity despite their high light transmission, yet the physical origin of this scattering has not been established. Here, polarization-resolved measurements reveal a pronounced polarization dependence of scattering by a wood-polymer composite with improved refractive index matching. Polarization- and spectrally-resolved haze as low as 21% (40-45% at 550 nm for unpolarized light) with transmittance of approximately 92% for polarization perpendicular to the fibers was detected. It is found that the low-haze spectrum closely follows an inverse-square relation over the 400-800 nm range, well described by a weak-index-contrast Rayleigh-Gans-Debye (RGD) model invoking subwavelength birefringent heterogeneities within the cell wall. This physical mechanism was previously obscured by haze-limiting strong scattering from debonding gaps or refraction at the lumen-cell wall interface. Scanning electron diffraction independently reveals spatially distinct domains with markedly different cellulose diffraction responses within the infiltrated cell walls. The observed polarization-dependent refractive-index mismatch is attributed to inherent cellulose birefringence. Time-resolved measurements further support nearly scattering-free quasi-ballistic transport of the sampled transmitted light. It is demonstrated that selecting only a preferential polarization markedly improves image visibility through TW without further material modification. These findings connect polarization-dependent haze to the internal structure of transparent wood and identify ways to engineer a refractive-index match in hierarchical anisotropic composites towards glass-like clarity.
item.dc:creator: Zheheng Song, Hui Chen, Mathias Nero, Jingjian Zhou, Ravi Shanker, Tom Willhammar, Lars Berglund, Ilya Sychugov

item.title: Deep-Microscopic Photonic Bandstructure of a Two-Dimensional Honeycomb Lattice
item.description: arXiv:2610.33709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional descriptions of light in materials rely on macroscopic models that average the optical response over the microscopic lattice structures. These models are deployed in the semi-classical limit, where the collective local response over many lattice sites is adequate. However, they fail to capture the full spatial dispersion, which requires a lattice-resolved description of light. We address this limitation by formulating a deep-microscopic nonlocal theory of the photon based on the Maxwell Hamiltonian and its characteristic equation. The solution reveals the full spatial dispersion in the form of deep-microscopic photonic bandstructure, and corresponding real-space Bloch field textures. We demonstrate our theory for a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a gapped honeycomb lattice. Our framework thus extends photons to the same microscopic footing as electrons or phonons, providing a unified route to studying topology, dissipation, and quantum fluctuations of light in dispersive materials.
item.dc:creator: Pronoy Das, Sathwik Bharadwaj, Wenbo Sun, Zubin Jacob

item.title: Optical imaging with only the evanescent fields and without diffraction
item.description: arXiv:2610.33720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on a conceptual framework for optical imaging utilizing exclusively evanescent fields, effectively eliminating or attenuating standard optical diffraction. We present the theoretical foundation of this concept based on the decomposition of dipole radiation into evanescent fields and homogeneous propagating waves, exploring the explicit conditions required to suppress the latter. By successfully decoupling and removing the homogeneous component, optical tasks, such as sub-diffraction imaging, can be executed solely via evanescent channels, bypassing traditional diffractive limits. We discuss the physical feasibility of this approach and provide concrete examples of how this conjecture can be realized using currently available laboratory and industrial techniques. The realization of this concept promises to redefine core paradigms in optics and fundamental physics. Because the minimum achievable feature size is no longer governed by the operating wavelength, this approach enables an unprecedented increase in spatial resolution, offering a direct pathway to advance state-of-the-art semiconductor lithography and chip manufacturing.
item.dc:creator: Mufei Xiao

item.title: Accurate measurement of Lithium Tantalate birefringence in whispering gallery resonators
item.description: arXiv:2610.33855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lithium Tantalate (LTA) is an important ferroelectric crystal widely used in piezoelectric, electro-optic, and nonlinear optical devices. Although this crystal is very common, there is an ongoing debate regarding its birefringence magnitude, and even its sign. While some sources claim it to be negative, others maintain that it is positive. The issue is further complicated by the sample-to-sample variation in the crystal composition, ranging from congruent to stoichiometric. Here we report the experimental exploration of this question based on high-resolution spectroscopy of optical whispering gallery resonators fabricated from this crystal. These sensitive measurements unambiguously indicate that in the near-infrared range at room temperature the stoichiometric LTA is negative, while the congruent LTA is positive.
item.dc:creator: Linjie Shao, Andrey B. Matsko, Anatoliy A. Savchenkov, Harald G. L. Schwefel, Nicholas J. Lambert, Florian Sedlmeir, Dmitry V. Strekalov

item.title: Non-Hermitian Topology of a Subwavelength Resonator in Synthetic Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.33871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian singularities and the nontrivial topology of energy bands have been extensively explored in extended periodic systems, where phenomena such as exceptional points and bulk Fermi arcs are naturally associated with periodicity and momentum space. Here, we show that this non-Hermitian topology can be extended to the domain of subwavelength resonators using a synthetic space. By reconstructing the complex energy bands of a subwavelength ring resonator in the synthetic space of geometrical parameters, we experimentally observe a spectral triplet formed by two exceptional points (EPs) connected by a bulk Fermi arc and a topologically robust quasi-bound state in the continuum (q-BIC). This Fermi-arc q-BIC emerges exactly at the intersection of the bulk Fermi arc and the q-BIC line in synthetic space, establishing a direct topological link between two spectral singularities. Encircling the EPs in synthetic space visualizes the nontrivial topology of the complex energy-band structure and reveals the opposite half-integer topological charges of the EPs connected by the bulk Fermi arc. These results extend non-Hermitian topology to subwavelength structures and establish compact resonators as a versatile platform for applications in photonics, microwave physics, and acoustics.
item.dc:creator: N. Solodovchenko, F. Zhang, M. Bochkarev, K. Samusev, M. Song, M. Limonov, A. Bogdanov

item.title: Surface Functionalization with Lasers: from Nanostructures to Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.33888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pulsed laser sources stand out as remarkable and versatile tools in the growing interdisciplinary field of materials science, offering capabilities for tailoring and customizing materials to meet specific requirements. Their ability to induce different controlled material alterations allows enhancing material properties that might otherwise remain elusive. In essence, laser-induced material modifications encompass a spectrum of transformative processes, ranging from subtle topographical changes in the nano- and microscale, to intricate chemical modifications. Among the challenges to overcome are the creation of approaches that allow tuning the properties of light to optimize interactions on various types of solids, including metals, semiconductors, and dielectrics. Understanding these interactions is paramount towards efficiency increase of the processing techniques. This chapter embarks on a comprehensive exploration of the intricate dance between pulsed laser beams and their interaction with matter at the surface. The applications of laser-induced surface modifications are far-reaching and extend into widespread industrial fields. Examples of these include tribology, where the study of friction, wear, and lubrication is paramount. Besides that, the modified surfaces find applications in wetting phenomena, changing surface energy and contact angle control, enhanced welding processes, and optimizing molecular adhesion for stronger and durable interfaces. The ability to precisely engineer material surface properties through laser processing opens new frontiers in materials and surface sciences, offering innovative solutions and pushing the boundaries of what can be achieved in various industrial and technological domains.
item.dc:creator: Bastian Zielinski, Martin Kahlmeyer, Stefan B\"ohm, J\"orn Bonse, Camilo Florian

item.title: Compressive microendoscopy in the presence of noise and misalignment: the translational correlation advantage of graded-index fibers
item.description: arXiv:2610.33933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimode fibers (MMFs) offer a minimally invasive platform for deep-tissue and multisite in vivo optical sensing. Computational microendoscopy methods extend them into the high-resolution imaging domain, but are quite sensitive to experimental errors. This study investigates the robustness of microendoscopy based on compressive sensing (CS) by comparing step-index (SI) MMFs with graded-index (GRIN) fibers. Mode-expansion-based simulations are used to assess the accuracy of image reconstruction in the presence of fundamental photon noise and lateral fiber shifts. We show that both fiber types exhibit comparable noise sensitivity, but GRIN fibers are significantly more robust to lateral misalignment errors. These results establish GRIN MMFs as an alignment-tolerant platform for robust computational microendoscopy.
item.dc:creator: M. S. Pochechuev, T. I. Rajib, A. Dharmasiri, A. M. Zheltikov

item.title: Nonreciprocal magneto-optic beam steering of thermal emission
item.description: arXiv:2610.33935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which ties absorptivity to emissivity and places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies and sensing systems. This constraint can be overcome using magneto-optic materials, which exhibit nonreciprocal thermal emission under an applied magnetic field. While the spectral nonreciprocity of magneto-optic devices has been explored theoretically and experimentally, nonreciprocal control over the direction of thermal emission has received far less attention. Here, we propose and numerically demonstrate nonreciprocal beam steering of thermal emission, wherein an applied magnetic field lifts the degeneracy between guided modes at +/- kx, enabling asymmetric and tunable directional thermal emission. We highlight a III-V semiconductor photonic structure operating at 24.5 um, a wavelength with few laser sources. This structure exhibits a nonreciprocity greater than 0.5 between +/- 75 degrees at 50 mT, a peak emissivity asymmetry over 0.6 at 150 mT, and 22 degrees of beam steering between 0 and 1 T. Our approach provides a solid-state means of steering a thermal beam, offering a potential route to magnetically controlled beam scanning of incandescent sources.
item.dc:creator: Mason Christiansen, Daniel Cui, Aaswath P. Raman

item.title: Functional Superoscillations in a Wave Processor
item.description: arXiv:2610.34111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical wave processors are constrained by diffraction, but the bandwidth of the mathematical functions they implement need not be set by it. Here, we demonstrate continuous and multiplexed optical processing of superoscillatory functions, in which a scalar argument is encoded onto a wavefront and a fixed diffractive wave processor synthesizes optical responses that approximate the corresponding function outputs in parallel. Unlike conventional superoscillatory optics that generates predetermined fields, superoscillation here is expressed in the input-output dependence on the encoded argument. Its frequencies are therefore distinct from the transverse spatial frequencies of propagating light and are not subject to the same diffraction-imposed cutoff. We demonstrate complex-valued superoscillatory function synthesis and introduce a multiplexed architecture that simultaneously evaluates distinct target superoscillatory functions whose harmonic content exceeds that of the optical input encoding. Visible-light experiments further validate this beyond-encoding superoscillatory regime. Together, these results establish functional superoscillation as a design principle for wave-based computation and show how interference, diffractive depth and spatial channel allocation extend the functional reach of passive wave processors. More broadly, these analyses establish a separation between functional bandwidth and physical wave bandwidth in analog optical computation.
item.dc:creator: Yuntian Wang, Md Sadman Sakib Rahman, Aydogan Ozcan

item.title: Axion Quasibound States in the Continuum and Their Enhanced Axion Nonlinearity
item.description: arXiv:2610.34195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical axion quasiparticles (DAQs) in condensed-matter systmes have emerged as a fascinating platform for exploring axion physics and nonlinear optical phenomena. However, the amplitude of the coherent oscillating $\theta$ field is even smaller than that of the static counterpart, making the experimental observation of DAQs particularly challenging. Here, we introduce symmetry-sensitive bound states in the continuum (BICs) physics to enable the all-optical detection of DAQs and enhance DAQ-mediated second-harmonic generation (SHG). Specifically, we uncover that DAQs induce optical shear that breaks the $C_{2z}$ symmetry of metagratings without geometric engineering, thereby converting symmetry-protected BICs into axion quasi-BICs (qBICs). In this context, the evolution of the quality factor and topological charge in momentum space, together with the appearance of optical resonances in far field associated with axion qBICs, offers achiral optical signatures for DAQ detection beyond the widely used Kerr and Faraday effects. Furthermore, by exploiting axion qBICs in the critical coupling regime to enhance fundamental optical field, we show that the SHG efficiency can be enhanced more than $10^5$-fold compared to bulk axion materials, achieving a conversion efficiency exceeding $10^{-6}~W^{-1}$. The SHG is governed by the magnetoelectric coupling, which differs from that in conventional SHG materials. Our findings establish a new approach for probing DAQs via achiral optical effects, while providing a versatile route for reconfigurable photonics and terahertz nonlinear optics.
item.dc:creator: Chang-Yin Ji, Chong Wang, Jiafang Li, Yugui Yao

item.title: Yb/Sr optical clock comparison at 2.2E-18 uncertainty over a 1350-km fiber link
item.description: arXiv:2610.34250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Redefining the International system of Units (SI) second requires independent frequency-ratio measurements between clocks based on different laboratories, with an overall uncertainty below 5E-18, to validate individual clock evaluations through consistency checks. Reaching this uncertainty over long distances has remained challenging. So far, comparisons at this level have been achieved only a few times, between co-located clocks, and their results disagree markedly. Previous high-precision comparisons have therefore been limited to local or kilometre-scale links. Here we compare a ytterbium optical lattice clock in Wuhan with a strontium optical lattice clock in Shanghai over a phase-stabilized fiber link spanning 1350 km, and determine the Yb/Sr frequency ratio to be 1.207 507 039 343 337 716 0(26), with a Bayesian statistical uncertainty of 1.14E-18 and a total uncertainty of 2.18E-18. To our knowledge, this is the first intercity long distance frequency-ratio measurement, whose total uncertainty reaches the level required by the redefinition roadmap. The measured ratio exhibits a significant correlation with Earth tides and its response agree with the model within the statistical uncertainty. At intercity scale, this comparison demonstrates the capability of an optical-clock network for frequency comparison and Earths gravitational-potential sensing, a key step toward a wide-area optical-clock network.
item.dc:creator: Lei Hou, Xiang-Pei Liu, Zhuan-Xian Xiong, Fa-Xi Chen, Wen-Xuan Song, Jian-Yu Guan, Qiang Zhu, Yu-Chen Zhang, Xiang Zhang, Bing Wang, De-Zhi Xiong, De-Quan Kong, Jia-Hao Zhang, Long-Fei Liao, Shao-Mao Wang, Xing-Yang Cui, Ping Xu, Peng Liu, Jie Li, Xiao Jiang, Ling-Xiang He, Li-Bo Li, Qi Shen, Youchao Xie, Lei Wang, Sheng-Kai Liao, Juan Yin, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Wen-Bin Shen, Bao-Long Lu, Han-Ning Dai, Yu-Ao Chen, Qiang Zhang, Hai-Feng Jiang, Jian-Wei Pan

item.title: High-speed laser speckle contrast imaging of the human retina
item.description: arXiv:2610.34605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate real-time laser speckle contrast imaging of the human retina using a Phantom S980 streaming camera at $3840\times2160$ pixels, 8-bit depth, and 1000 frames per second, with a $988\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ exposure. We report four recordings of the peripapillary retina around the optic disc in the right eye of one healthy 25-year-old emmetropic man, acquired without pharmacological pupil dilation, using 852-nm diffuse Maxwellian illumination at an entering optical power of 5.0 mW. Each recording contained 4096 frames (4.10 s), and all 16384 frames in the reported recordings were retained. Open-source Holoflow software on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 computes $K=\sigma/\mu$ over $5\times5$ spatial pixels and nonoverlapping blocks of 16 frames, producing 62.5 contrast maps/s with 60-frame/s rendering and no additional averaging. The nominal raw-input throughput is 8.29 Gpixel/s. Main retinal arterial and venous branches and smaller peripapillary vessels were visualized. Variations during the cardiac cycle were visible in the principal retinal arteries and veins, as illustrated in the Supplementary Videos. Regional inverse-contrast traces show an arterial dicrotic notch and spontaneous venous pulsation. This single-volunteer demonstration establishes an operating point for high-throughput retinal speckle-contrast visualization. Physiological observations are descriptive; contrast is an instrument-dependent observable rather than a calibrated blood-flow velocity.
item.dc:creator: Zacharie Auray, Jules Guillou, Basile Malbois, Maxime Boy-Arnould, Michael Atlan

item.title: Physical Adjoint Learning in Wave Systems with Asymmetric Couplings
item.description: arXiv:2610.34815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing self-optimizing physical systems that learn directly from their response to external stimuli offers a promising route toward adaptive and intelligent machines. A key ingredient is the ability to evaluate optimization gradients within the physical hardware, bypassing the need for accurate numerical models. In wave systems, \textit{in-situ} adjoint methods provide this capability by exploiting reciprocity to physically realize the adjoint dynamics. However, this approach generally breaks down in nonreciprocal systems, where the adjoint field cannot be directly accessed through the original device. Here, we develop an \textit{in-situ} adjoint optimization framework that extends physical gradient computation to wave systems with asymmetric couplings through computationally low-cost similarity transformations between the forward and transposed operators. We utilize available degrees of freedom like tailored injected excitations, targeted measurements, and tunable parameters, to enable adjoint field reconstruction through forward experiments on the same physical platform. We demonstrate the versatility of the protocol through broadband transmission and isolation, coherent perfect absorption, programmable wavefront shaping, and spatially selective sensing. Our results provide a route to self-optimization in complex nonreciprocal wave systems through efficient physical gradient-based learning. The number of experiments required by the protocol does not increase with the number of optimization parameters, and the method remains applicable even when parts of the system are completely inaccessible.
item.dc:creator: Lucas J. Fern\'andez-Alc\'azar, John Guillamon, Krishna Joshi, Tsampikos Kottos

item.title: Electro-optic comb-driven massive data transmission on monolithically integrated lithium niobate photonic circuits
item.description: arXiv:2610.34821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven by large AI models, the demand for datacenter interconnects is outstripping traditional scaling laws. This necessitates a transition toward dense multiplexing techniques, such as wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM), for datacenter environments, transferring long-haul spectral efficiency to short-reach, high-bandwidth applications. Integrated optical frequency combs offer compact, low-cost light sources for future datacenter WDM interconnects. However, existing Kerr comb and mode-locked laser implementations suffer from drawbacks in power efficiency, spectral flatness and phase noise. Their fixed, device-specific channel spacings often conflict with standard WDM grids, and co-integration with high-speed modulators remains challenging. Here, we overcome these limitations by demonstrating high-capacity data transmission using flat-top electro-optic combs on thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN), a platform featuring flat spectra, tunable wavelengths and comb spacing, alongside native compatibility with (de-)multiplexers and high-speed modulators. Using 46 wavelength channels from two lasers and a 50-GHz on-chip electro-optic comb, we realize 16.56 Tb/s coherent transmission over a 98.84-km deployed fiber link between two universities and two datacenters in Hong Kong, verifying its suitability for inter-datacenter connections. To highlight grid reconfigurability, we reconfigure the comb to 100-GHz spacing via an on-chip demultiplexer and demonstrate 10-channel, 80-GBaud coherent transmission at 6.4 Tb/s. We further report a proof-of-concept monolithic WDM transmitter integrating the comb and high-speed modulator, achieving 19-channel, 45-GBaud IM/DD transmission at 1.71 Tb/s. Our work validates TFLN electro-optic combs as flexible, compact and scalable WDM engines for both coherent and IM/DD datacenter links to satisfy rapidly rising bandwidth requirements.
item.dc:creator: Yikun Chen, Chuang Xu, Ke Zhang, Xiong Wu, Kangping Zhong, Xiangzhi Xie, Hanke Feng, Yifan Wu, Chao Lu, Alan Pak Tao Lau, Cheng Wang

item.title: Why Emission Spectral Profile of Diverse Fluoro-phores Look Alike with Thick Polymer Overlayers?
item.description: arXiv:2610.34864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluorescence from fluorophore-polymer overlayers reflects an interplay between molecular photo-physics and thickness dependent optical propagation. Combining spectrally resolved single mole-cule measurements, transition dipole moment orientation analysis and ensemble fluorescence, we show that structurally and photophysically distinct fluorophores can exhibit similar red shifted emission profiles under thick polymer overlayers even without additional reflecting surface. This similarity indicates a common optical transfer function imposed by the overlayer rather than a pure-ly fluorophore specific molecular response. Although local molecular interactions, excited state dy-namics and vibronic coupling govern intrinsic emission, the overlayer modifies detected spectra through refractive index contrast, dielectric boundary reflections, cavity effects and collection ge-ometry. Vibronic energy spacing distributions remain largely preserved as thickness changes, whereas spectral positions and relative intensities vary systematically. Thus, polymer thickness pri-marily reshapes detected spectrum through optical propagation and outcoupling while retaining vi-brational modes. Time dependent density functional theory identifies candidate Franck-Condon and Herzberg-Teller active dye modes contributing to spectral fluctuations and dipole reorientation.
item.dc:creator: Vinayak Kumar Tiwari, Srishti Batra, Aranyak Sarkar, Vinu Namboodiri, Ravindra Venka-tramani, Manoj Kumbhakar

item.title: Data-efficient linear hyperspectral imaging through risk-guided co-design
item.description: arXiv:2610.34935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational hyperspectral imaging reconstructs spatial-spectral information from limited optical measurements. Linear reconstructors are efficient and interpretable, but often underperform deep nonlinear models, which typically require substantial training data and computational resources. Here we present a theory-guided encoding-reconstruction co-design framework that achieves, to our knowledge, state-of-the-art linear reconstruction performance. We establish a theory for the exact five-term decomposition of reconstruction risk and introduce a method for diagnosing the statistical-coverage lower bound within a fixed principal component analysis envelope, which together inform the optimized design of hyperspectral imaging systems. The framework applies across coded-aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI), diffractive optical element imaging and spectral filter array imaging, achieving 34.76 dB mean PSNR in single-shot CASSI, outperforming a deep baseline by 9.43 dB with only five source scenes, and matching empirical cross-domain risk within 0.2%. Our results establish a data-efficient and theoretically grounded route to high-performance linear hyperspectral reconstruction, while providing a quantitative basis for identifying whether reconstruction is limited by optical encoding, reconstruction design or statistical coverage.
item.dc:creator: Shenzhan Hong, Shuxing Yang, Taojun Ying, Fujia Chen, Zongyin Yang, Hongsheng Chen, Yihao Yang

item.title: Analysis of C-point and V-point Inhomogeneous Vector Beams Stability under Anisotropic Turbulence in Ground-to-Air Transmission
item.description: arXiv:2610.35116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the present work, we explore the impact of anisotropic turbulence on the propagation characteristics of polarization singular LG and circular Airy vector beams along vertical, oblique, and horizontal transmission configurations. The influence of altitude-dependent turbulence anisotropy on beam evolution is assessed through changes in intensity distribution and degradation of spatial structure. Polarization characteristics of the propagated fields exhibiting C-point and V-point polarization singularities are quantified using the Stokes parameter framework, from which the degree of polarization is derived based on ensemble-averaged electric field correlations. To further interpret polarization dynamics, the corresponding Stokes vectors are mapped onto the higher order Poincar\'e sphere, providing a geometric visualization of turbulence-driven depolarization and polarization state dispersion. Numerical simulations have shown that the anisotropy of turbulence significantly enhances the polarization instability. Horizontal and slant-path propagations suffer stronger depolarization and polarization-state diffusion than vertical propagation. These results demonstrate the importance of vectorial polarization analysis in describing the propagation of a structured beam in real atmospheric environments. Overall, C-point polarization singularities of circular Airy vector beams are found to be the most resistant to turbulence-induced intensity fluctuation and polarization degradation in anisotropic atmospheric conditions.
item.dc:creator: Sagar, Sanjay Kumar Mishra, Akhilesh Kumar Mishra

item.title: Effects of Pulse Duration on Kerr Self-Focusing and Weld Formation in Ultrafast Laser Welding of Fused Silica
item.description: arXiv:2610.35250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kerr self-focusing can shift the laser interaction region away from the geometrical focus, making energy deposition near the joining interface difficult to control. Here, the effect of pulse duration on nonlinear focusing and weld formation is investigated from 262 fs to 10 ps. ICCD imaging shows clear changes in the axial position and shape of the plasma emission. Different pulse durations already produce distinct axial positions during the initial 2000 pulses, and these positions continue to evolve with pulse accumulation. The final weld morphology, weld position, and shear strength show corresponding changes. A ray-optics model including the Kerr effect is used to calculate the focal shift. The simulated trend agrees with the experiment and supports the role of Kerr self-focusing in the observed focal position change. These results clarify the relationship between pulse duration, nonlinear focusing, interaction position, and weld formation.
item.dc:creator: Chen Yitong, Li Nan, Han Zhijie, Li Yuxuan, Zhang Qingwei, Dong Zihui, Sun Yuming, Lin Zhe, Zhu Gangyi, Yang Shanglu

item.title: HarP: a simulation tool for high-order harmonic generation and propagation in gases
item.description: arXiv:2610.35440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurately simulating high-order harmonic generation (HHG) for attosecond science requires connecting the microscopic single-atom quantum dynamics and the macroscopic propagation of intense driving laser fields. HarP is an open-source Python code designed to address this multiscale problem. It solves the wave equations for both the driving laser field and the generated harmonics, using precomputed dipole tables for the nonlinear polarization density. This tabulation enables the direct integration of accurate microscopic models while avoiding costly calculations during the propagation. The methodology builds upon the approach of [L'Huillier et al. (1992) PRA 46, 2778] and has already facilitated multiple studies on phase matching, propagation effects and HHG optimization. This paper presents the underlying physical model, its numerical implementation, and comparison against alternative simulation frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Mattys Pouyez, Dominika Maslarova, Linus Hagedorn, Patrik Jansson, Robin Weissenbilder, Stefanos Carlstr\"om, Anne L'Huillier, T\"unde F\"ul\"op

item.title: Parameter-Decoupling-Informed Learning for Superresolution: Laboratory Validation and Galaxy Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.35449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a parameter-decoupling-informed learning model for estimating subwavelength separations of point sources, without requiring prior knowledge of source properties, control over the sources, or continued access to their light signals. The method builds on our parameter-decoupled quantum superresolution estimation theory, which circumvents the need to estimate nuisance parameters such as partial coherence, brightness imbalance, and relative phase. Our convolutional neural network further accommodates practical imperfections, including background noise, photon loss, and centroid and orientation misalignment. We validate the method using synthetic and experimentally generated images, achieving separation-estimation fidelity above $82\%$ for separations as small as approximately $0.075\sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the Gaussian intensity-PSF standard deviation. This corresponds to an illustrative separation of $\sim13.5$ nm when $\sigma=180$ nm, suggesting potential relevance to length scales addressed by advanced active-source microscopy. Applied to archival Hubble images of NGC~4486B, the model yields nuclear separations of 9.3-13.2~pc, consistent with the previously reported value of 12~pc. Comparisons using the same training and testing images demonstrate substantially higher fidelity than conventional direct data-driven learning in the tested cases. The method's robustness to varying source properties and imaging imperfections supports retrospective astrophysical image analysis and motivates applications in live-cell microscopy and quantum metrology where source control or renewed optical measurements are impractical.
item.dc:creator: Abdelali Sajia, Bilal Benzimoun, James Qu, Pawan Khatiwada, Guogan Zhao, Gang Zhang, Xiao-Feng Qian

item.title: Optical Speckle Patterns as Nonlinear Feature Maps for Photonic Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.35546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for energy-efficient hardware, and optical computing has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional electronic processors owing to its high parallelism and potentially lower power consumption. In this work, we investigate an optical computing architecture based on an integrated photonic circular multipass cell, focusing on its suitability for machine learning and pattern recognition tasks. The properties of the system are evaluated through measures of nonlinearity and cosine similarity, which characterize the system's information-processing capacity and the dimensionality of the generated feature representations. Numerical results demonstrate that the reservoir mirror reflectance, the size of the encoded figure, and the refractive-index contrast between the reservoir and the encoded figure modify the nonlinearity of the system, as verified via pairwise similarity estimates. These results indicate that the features generated by the circular multipass cell can be tailored by adjusting the system parameters, providing a means to control the reservoir transformation of the input data. The resulting representations were applied to classification tasks involving texture images and thyroid collagen images, achieving classification accuracies ranging from 69% to 93%. These findings suggest that photonic computing systems could provide a basis for more energy-efficient machine-learning hardware.
item.dc:creator: Kiia Arola, Mikko J. Huttunen

item.title: Transverse detuned loading for modulation bandwidth enhancement in VCSELs
item.description: arXiv:2610.35578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Directly modulated vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs) are central to short-reach optical interconnects, where modulation bandwidth and power efficiency are critical factors for increasing data transfer capacity. Conventional oxide VCSELs still require power-hungry signal processing to achieve high-speed data transmission above 100 Gb/s. Here we report an experimental implementation of detuned loading in a VCSEL to enhance the modulation bandwidth. The detuned loading is achieved by carrier-induced index variations that reshape an engineered transverse mode so its overlap with spatially selective optical losses decreases with increased carrier density. This produces a negative differential loss reminiscent of that in detuned-loaded DBR lasers lasing on the long-wavelength reflectivity flank. The resulting 850 nm single-mode VCSEL exhibits an enhanced carrier-photon relaxation frequency of 44 GHz, yielding a 3dB electrical modulation bandwidth exceeding 50 GHz. The enhancement persists from 25 {\deg}C to 75 {\deg}C showing the robustness of the mechanism introduced. The same device supports 106.25 Gb/s NRZ transmission without digital signal processing, transmitter pre-emphasis or receiver equalization. These results establish transverse detuned loading as a robust alternative approach for extending the modulation bandwidth of vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Graziano, Richard Schatz, Antoine Pissis, Wilfried Maineult, Aurelio Rossinelli, Philipp T\"aschler, Simon H\"onl, Vincenzo Pasanisi, Tobias S\"uss, Dario Schiavon, Donato Bonfrate, Martin Spieser, Stefano Tirelli, Evgeny Zibik

item.title: Chirpons: elementary local phase oscillations associated with complex zeros
item.description: arXiv:2610.35599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a complex wave, the local phase variation provides the instantaneous frequency in time, the local wavenumber in space, and the local momentum in quantum mechanics. Here we study this quantity from the complex-zero structure of the analytic continuation of the wave. A single nonreal zero produces a localized Lorentzian phase variation on the real axis, whose position, width, sign, amplitude, and integrated phase are fixed by the zero itself. We call this elementary zero-associated oscillation a chirpon. The representation is exact for finite products and finite Fourier sums, and extends to entire and band-limited functions through canonical factorization. We illustrate the construction with superoscillatory sequences and discrete Fourier sums, showing how local anomalous oscillations can be reconstructed from periodic families of complex zeros. We further show how linear systems transform chirpons through the displacement of their associated complex zeros, and illustrate this dynamics for quadratic dispersive propagation and a resonant harmonic oscillator. This establishes a direct relation between local phase structure and the amplitude and phase response of the transfer function, suggesting a zero-based form of spectroscopy in which system parameters can be inferred from the motion, width, and orientation of chirpons. More broadly, the chirpon description provides a unified framework for instantaneous frequency, local wavenumber, superoscillation, backflow, and other local phase phenomena, while offering a new route for probing linear systems through the dynamics of their complex zeros.
item.dc:creator: Enrique G Neyra, Laureano A Bulus Rossini, Pablo A Costanzo Caso, Marcelo F Ciappina, Lorena Reb\'on

item.title: Plasma and light: Shaping High Harmonic Generation in Time-Varying Media
item.description: arXiv:2610.35646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High harmonic generation in solids is typically described under the assumption of a stationary medium. This assumption is rarely questioned because the electronic properties of most media evolve on timescales much slower than the harmonic emission process itself. However, in strongly driven time-varying transparent conductive oxides the plasma frequency, carrier density, and effective mass can evolve on the same femtosecond timescale as harmonic generation. Under these conditions, harmonic generation and material evolution are no longer independent processes. Within this context, we consider a two-field pumping scheme in which a strong field generates a comb of high-order harmonics across a broad spectral window, while a weaker field simultaneously reshapes its own individual spectral lines. Distinct from geometry-dependent wave-mixing processes, the evolving electron plasma reshapes multiple collinear harmonic channels simultaneously. A fully self-consistent hydrodynamic-Maxwell framework reveals that even- and odd-order harmonics naturally emerge from free- and bound-electron dynamics without the typical need to invoke phenomenological nonlinearities. Our model captures the full spectral evolution on an ultra-broad bandwidth, while experiments performed on ITO confirm the distinct behavior of bulk-driven odd harmonics and interface-driven even harmonics under strong pumping. These results establish time-dependent plasma dynamics as a powerful new tool for broadband hyperspectral shaping of multiple harmonic channels beyond the framework of four-wave-mixing processes. Our findings are of particular relevance to ultrafast science, with potential applications in ultrafast pulse manipulation and the generation and control of tailored multi harmonic waveforms.
item.dc:creator: Wallace Jaffray, Maria Antonietta Vincenti, Domenico de Ceglia, Carlo Rizza, Natalia M. Litchinitser, Jose Trull, Crina Cojocaru, Marcello Ferrera, Michael Scalora

item.title: Theoretical description of high-harmonic spectroscopy for uniaxial nematic and isotropic liquid crystals
item.description: arXiv:2610.35672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enabled by their controllable optical anisotropy, liquid crystals form a cornerstone of linear optical and display technologies. Bringing the versatile platform into the nonlinear regime, we explore its nonlinear optical anisotropy by high-order harmonic generation spectroscopy. Through a comprehensive study targeting gas, liquid, nematic, and crystalline phases, we present a semi-empirical tight-binding approach that provides insight into the intermolecular character of ultrafast light-driven electron dynamics across soft-matter mesophases. We demonstrate how intermolecular electron hybridization enables spectroscopic access to structural properties, such as the nematic director and order parameter. Outlining such foundational mechanisms opens avenues towards nonlinear liquid crystal devices and ultrafast soft-matter spectroscopies.
item.dc:creator: Simon Vendelbo Bylling Jensen, Marta L. Murillo-S\'anchez, Andrea Annunziata, Angel Rubio, Laura Cattaneo, Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean

item.title: Daylight-Referenced Efficiency (DRE): A Radiometric Measure of Electric Light Source Efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2610.35746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photopic luminous efficacy (lm/W) weights optical power strictly against human eye sensitivity V (lambda), creating a systemic metrological penalty for electric light sources engineered with broad spectral output in the ultraviolet (280-380 nm) or infrared (780-4000 nm) bands. Similarly, metrics evaluating chromaticity, color quality, or melanopic pathways assess photoreceptor responses strictly within the visual band, offering no measure of broad-spectrum physical radiant power conversion. To resolve this limitation, we introduce Daylight-Referenced Efficiency (eta_DRE), a radiometric framework that evaluates how efficiently an electric light source converts electrical power into an optical spectrum matching natural terrestrial daylight across domain Omega = [280 nm, 4000 nm]. The framework factorizes performance into primary physical quantities: domain-restricted Wall-Plug Efficiency (eta_wall [W_optical/W_elec]), measuring unweighted electrical-to-optical conversion, and Daylight Spectral Fidelity (eta_spec [unitless, 0-1]), quantifying geometric shape match to the ASTM G173 AM1.5G solar reference via total variation distance (1 - TVD). Multiplying total optical power by spectral fidelity yields the absolute Daylight-Referenced Output Power (P_dr [W]), establishing a direct physical flux quantity for lighting specification. Dividing by electrical drive power gives the summary metric Daylight-Referenced Efficiency (eta_DRE = eta_wall * eta_spec [W/W_elec]), measuring net reference-conforming radiant output per electrical Watt consumed. The mathematical architecture is reference-agnostic, domain-extensible, and maintains provable lower-bound monotonicity for eta_wall and eta_DRE under spectral truncation. Open-source reference software is provided to facilitate deployment and standardized rating of broad-spectrum light sources.
item.dc:creator: Peter Veto

item.title: Tapering to Enhance the Performance of Nanowire-Based Fluorescent Biosensors
item.description: arXiv:2610.35791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-refractive-index nanowires are of interest for signal enhancement in fluorescence-based biosensing. Here, through electromagnetic modelling, we demonstrate substantial fluorescence signal enhancement by incorporating a tapered section into a cylindrical nanowire and investigate two complementary tapering configurations to address practical implementation challenges. Under near-normal excitation, the excitation enhancement increases approximately linearly with taper length, reaching more than three times that of the corresponding non-tapered nanowire at a taper length of 8000 nm. In a non-imaging signal detection scheme using a low numerical aperture (NA), the proposed tapered nanowire achieves more than three orders of magnitude enhancement in fluorescence signal compared with a planar biosensor. Thus, the tapered nanowire should enable efficient fluorescence detection using compact, low-NA optical configuration. In imaging mode, similarly as for non-tapered nanowires, imaging sharpness beyond conventional microscopy limitations is obtained when imaging from the non-tapered nanowire end, while strongly increased excitation enhancement is simultaneously obtained when exciting from the opposite, tapered end.
item.dc:creator: Farhana Akter Mou, Nicklas Anttu

item.title: Real Time Motion Detection in Video Inspired by Photonic Time Stretch
item.description: arXiv:2610.33351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Motion perception is fundamental to computer vision and physical AI, and plays a central role in robotics, autonomous vehicles, human-computer interaction, and video compression. Traditional approaches such as background subtraction, frame-differencing and optical flow algorithms often struggle in complex or dynamic scenes, typically sacrificing spatial resolution for computational tractability. Here we introduce MoViD (Motion estimation via Virtual dispersion and phase Detection), a physics-inspired algorithm grounded in the principles that govern photonic time stretch - a highly successful ultrafast realtime data acquisition platform. Drawing inspiration from the optical physics therein, MoViD treats video as a collection of optical time series waveforms associated with pixels. Motion of an object through a pixel broadens the time series spectrum and, after group delay dispersion, induces a temporal phase that exists only if there is motion. Spatiotemporal group delay dispersion templates, corresponding to dielectric functions, classify specific motion trajectories. Unlike conventional empirical phase-based motion-analysis pipelines that require narrow-band spatial channelization and pyramid reconstruction, the physics-based MoViD operates directly on the broadband video signal, vastly increasing its computational speed. The resulting algorithm achieves unprecedented performance in both motion characterization and motion magnification, providing full-resolution motion mapping in real time at nearly 200 frames per second at 4K resolution and 70 frames per second for 8K video - orders of magnitude faster than classical optical flow approaches or learning-based methods. Notably, such extreme performance enables real time motion analysis at ultrahigh resolution for motion detection and compensation in robotics and other autonomous devices.
item.dc:creator: Callen MacPhee, Yiming Zhou, Bahram Jalali

item.title: Krylov geometry and optimal recovery under uncertain coherent noise
item.description: arXiv:2610.33607v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recovery from a coherent rotation with an unobserved angle depends on both the encoding and what calibration reveals about the noise. We determine their combined limit for a known finite-dimensional generator and one final recovery. Two polynomial projections organize the answer. A physical Krylov chain separates correctable error amplitudes from their first state-dependent distortion; projection onto lower-angle powers identifies the part that a coherent decoder can cancel. Under explicit rank and moment conditions, their combination gives the exact leading optimal entanglement infidelity at weak noise and a recovery attaining it for any finite logical dimension. The optimal worst-input error lies between one and $d$ times that infidelity at leading order, for logical dimension $d$. When the angle distribution is unknown, we optimize one decoder for every distribution compatible with the calibration. When spectral and calibration frequencies are integer multiples of a common frequency, moment positivity turns this into an exact finite optimization. Small measured means can still allow rare finite rotations. If the sole calibration datum is $\beta_r=\mathbb E[\sin^{2r}(\theta/2)]$, with $\theta$ the wrapped rotation phase at that common frequency, the optimal worst-prior infidelity is $O(\beta_r)$ exactly when generator powers through degree $r-1$ are correctable. When the first uncorrectable power has degree $m<r$, the optimal loss scales as $\beta_r^{m/r}$, with a sharp coefficient fixed by a universal moment problem. In a loss-free four-photon memory, population measurements at two calibration durations retain the fully informed quartic error coefficient for a fixed symmetric narrow-noise family with positive variance and finite fourth moment; a single duration permits loss quadratic in the noise width.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Chowdhury

item.title: Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Network for Single-Shot 3D Reconstruction from Fringe Patterns
item.description: arXiv:2610.33988v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning facilitates rapid single shot three dimensional (3D) reconstruction using fringe projection profilometry (FPP), but recovering accurate surface height from a single high frequency fringe image remains challenging because both long-range spatial consistency and fine geometric details must be preserved. Convolutional networks are limited in modeling long range dependencies, whereas window-based Transformers establish global interactions only progressively with increasing depth. To address these limitations, a hybrid Mamba Transformer network is proposed for fringe to height regression. The network adopts a Swin based U shaped architecture and introduces visual state space modeling at the intermediate resolution encoder stage. An axial and dilated vision state space (ADVSS) block is further developed to enhance prescan feature encoding through local, dilated, and axial depthwise convolutions while retaining four directional selective scanning. This design combines linear complexity long range modeling with direction aware preservation of local fringe structures. Experiments on a publicly available FPP dataset show that the proposed method outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet in mean absolute error(MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), absolute relative error, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Using only one deformed fringe image, the proposed method achieves an RMSE of 0.548 mm and an SSIM of 0.9985, reducing RMSE by 65.2% and 59.6% relative to UHRNet and HiDNet, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining selective state space modeling with hierarchical window based attention for accurate single-shot FPP reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Xinjie Zhou, XiaoLei Li

item.title: Matter that learns what matters
item.description: arXiv:2610.34428v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a material learn what deserves its attention? We show that it can in a model optical network, in which action outcomes train a persistent record in each link. The record biases whether a source is consulted and sets how strongly it changes a stored answer, so useful sources gain attention and influence without being identified in advance. The network's experience thus shapes the information available for its future learning. Resonant readouts make this learning fragile: reinforcement can carry a record past resonance, where it persists but its influence weakens. We derive bounds within which relevant signals guide the answer, irrelevant signals are rejected and stored answers remain open to revision. These bounds guide a learning rule that limits reinforcement as records form; in simulations, it acquires useful records and keeps them functional. When relevance changes, an obsolete record can block its own replacement. A local state that strengthens negative writing after unsuccessful actions releases obsolete records and completes the learning sequence more often. How a memory is read should decide how it is written.
item.dc:creator: Natalia G. Berloff

item.title: Symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity
item.description: arXiv:2610.34637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nonreciprocity enriches wave control and information processing through directional transport, yet challenges conventional in-situ physical adjoint optimization, which relies on reciprocity to acquire adjoint responses. Here we demonstrate symmetry-driven in-situ physical adjoint computing (Sym-iPAC) in nonreciprocal systems, which enables access to adjoint responses on the original hardware through three classes of transpose symmetry: local geometric permutations, complex gauge reweighting, and latent symmetry in effective port dynamics revealed by Schur reduction. Experiments with programmable nonreciprocal microwave networks validate these transpose relations and yield adjoint gradients, enabling closed-loop optimization. These results establish experimentally accessible transpose symmetry as a route to in-situ physical adjoint computing beyond reciprocity.
item.dc:creator: Cunshen Li, Rong Li, Jiongning Che, Cheng-Zhen Wang, Liang Huang

item.title: Experimental Validation of Double-Blind Fourier Holography in an HWO-Like Segmented Aperture
item.description: arXiv:2610.34760v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Double-Blind Fourier Holography (DBFH) is a phase-retrieval method that has been shown numerically to address wavefront-sensing challenges for future segmented-aperture space telescopes, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). DBFH uses a set of carefully selected pupil-plane amplitude masks and their corresponding focal-plane intensity measurements to construct an algebraically linear inverse problem, enabling computationally efficient and stable reconstruction of the complex pupil field. Here, we present the first experimental demonstration of DBFH using a spatial light modulator and an HWO EAC5-like segmented-aperture geometry. We reconstruct challenging pseudo-random wavefronts and compare DBFH with the established Focus-Diverse Phase Retrieval (FDPR) method. The two methods achieve comparable reconstruction precision, while exhibiting distinct strengths and limitations. We further demonstrate DBFH wavefront sensing in the presence of a binary source, a scenario that is not naturally accommodated by conventional FDPR. These results provide experimental proof of concept and establish technology readiness level 3 for DBFH as a wavefront-sensing method for space telescopes with segmented primary mirrors.
item.dc:creator: Oren Pedatzur, Noah Schwartz, D. Scott Acton, Ben Buky

item.title: Parametrically Enhanced Ergotropy and Charging Power in a Three-Mode Bosonic Quantum Battery
item.description: arXiv:2610.35734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum batteries are quantum systems that potentially serve as fuel for other quantum devices by receiving and supplying energy. In this work, we propose a theoretical scheme to enhance ergotropy and charging power of quantum Battery in the system under consideration through squeezed light. Moreover, The system comprises a coherently driven charger cavity, a strongly dissipative auxiliary cavity acting as a mediator, and an energy--storage battery cavity. Quantum nonreciprocity and directional energy flow are established via destructive quantum interference between the direct coupling path and the loss--engineered indirect path. A degenerate optical parametric amplifier integrated into the charger cavity acts as an active, phase--sensitive energy source that injects two--photon quantum excitations and anomalous correlations. Using a strictly open--quantum--system framework derived directly from the Lindblad master equation, we obtain the full expectation--value dynamics and stationary states. We show that active parametric driving drastically increases the stored energy and peak charging power while maintaining nonreciprocal energy trapping in the battery. We achieve a multi-order-of-magnitude boost in the battery's stored energy, charging power, and ergotropy. We also analyze the effects of pure dephasing on the charging power, ergotropy, and extractable work quality.. Although two--photon pumping introduces photon--number fluctuations that slightly lower the fractional ergotropy ratio ${\cal W}_{\rm B}/{\cal E}_{\rm B}$, the absolute extractable work remains substantially elevated compared to unassisted configurations.
item.dc:creator: Mustapha Tarboun, Mohamed Amazioug

item.title: Interaction-Induced Topological Transport of Extended Doublons
item.description: arXiv:2507.12131v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Topological boundary states are a defining feature of topological systems, providing robust transport protected against perturbations. While such states are commonly engineered in non-interacting systems, how to realize interaction-induced topological states composed of only few particles has remained experimentally unexplored thus far. In this work, we realize such states using a driven photonic lattice as a linear analogue platform. We observe the formation of spatially extended bound states of two interacting particles, in which the particles remain correlated while occupying different lattice sites. At discrete values of the local interaction, these bound states support robust transport governed by a topological phase arising from drive-induced correlated hopping. Our results establish an experimentally accessible route to interaction-driven topology beyond single-particle physics and provide a versatile framework for exploring correlated few-particle phenomena across different physical platforms.
item.dc:creator: Julius Beck, Matthias Heinrich, Marcus J. Meschede, Helena Dr\"ueke, Francesco S. Piccioli, Sebastian Weidemann, Joshua Feis, Dieter Bauer, Alexander Szameit

item.title: Ultra-broadband Mid to Long-wave Infrared Spintronic Poisson Bolometer
item.description: arXiv:2601.11733v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Infrared detectors have traditionally been divided into two fundamental classes, mid-wave (MWIR, 3-5 um) and long-wave (LWIR, 8-14 um). Integrating MWIR and LWIR within a single device is challenging due to distinct materials, cooling needs, and detection mechanisms, while such integration is critical for improved object recognition, temperature estimation, and environmental sensing. In this work, we demonstrate a Spintronic Poisson (SP) bolometer enabling room-temperature ultra-broadband sensing across 3-14 um. Unlike conventional bolometers that rely on continuous analog signals, the SP bolometer implements a Poisson-counting detection paradigm, encoding temperature in discrete stochastic events, which turns thermal noise from a limitation into the basis of the estimator itself. We fabricate the SP bolometer using a spintronic transduction layer integrated with a plasmonic nanoantenna array to enhance broadband infrared absorption. Using spintronic transduction, the device achieves the noise-equivalent temperature difference (NETD, thermal sensitivity metric) of 80-100 mK at 300 K, surpassing uncooled detectors and approaching cooled technologies. This work establishes a statistical detection paradigm for room-temperature infrared sensing with broad application potential.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed A. Mousa, Leif Bauer, Daien He, Sakshi Gupta, Shubhankar Jape, Utkarsh Singh, Bhagwati Prasad, Partha P. Mukherjee, Angshuman Deka, Zubin Jacob

item.title: Design and Optimization of Metasurfaces for Silicon Photonics: PhD Thesis
item.description: arXiv:2607.21091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Metasurfaces, two-dimensional arrangements of subwavelength nanopillars, provide local control over the phase of light, enabling flat optical functions beyond conventional refractive components. Their inverse design, finding the pillar distribution producing a target response, faces two obstacles: the immense dimensionality of the design space and the prohibitive cost of rigorous electromagnetic simulations, precluding exhaustive exploration at device scale. This thesis addresses the challenge in three stages. The first assesses the reliability of rigorous Maxwell solvers: comparing three implementations of Li's factorization rules for RCWA shows that spectral convergence does not guarantee physical fidelity, as these rules implicitly distort the simulated permittivity, most severely in the plasmonic regime. FDTD, immune to such artifacts, is retained as ground truth throughout. The second stage removes the computational bottleneck: a local phase-approximation model, then fully convolutional surrogates trained on FDTD simulations of large pillar metasurfaces, predict the near field almost instantaneously. Exploiting problem symmetries quadruples the training database, and the surrogates generalize to much larger apertures while remaining differentiable. The third stage benchmarks three strategies under a common FDTD protocol ($R^2$ between realized and target far fields): Gerchberg-Saxton retrieval and Local Model ($R^2\approx0.925$), surrogate-based and heuristic-initialized gradient descent ($R^2\approx0.975$), and a generative framework based on diffusion models and Schr\"odinger bridges. Hybrid posterior sampling and amplitude constraints restore scale-invariant fidelity on surfaces over 230 times larger than training, with diverse, fabrication-tolerant designs. Database enhancement lifts every approach to $R^2\approx0.97$.
item.dc:creator: Mathys Le Grand (Institut des Nanotechnologies de Lyon, STMicroelectronics)

item.title: Multiphysics simulation of all-optical switching and sequential magneto-optic readout in an integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/GdFeCo waveguide
item.description: arXiv:2608.22969v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In an integrated all-optical magnetic device, a guided pulse writes a magnetic state and a later optical signal reads it out. We study both steps for an 8 nm GdFeCo film inserted across a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide. A three-dimensional dispersive finite-difference time-domain calculation gives the energy absorbed from an 800 nm pump pulse. This energy drives a four-temperature model and calibrated stochastic two-sublattice Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch dynamics. After relaxation, a separate 532 nm probe is propagated through the fixed magnetic state for the optical readout. At the reference pump fluence, the model reverses 0.859 of the film from either saturated state. The switched fraction remains within 0.81-0.87 over a 2.4-fold range of incident fluence. A threshold rule applied to the local absorption map reproduces the five three-dimensional simulation points to within $8\times10^{-4}$, showing that, within the model, incomplete reversal results from non-uniform guided-mode absorption. When the film starts from zero magnetization, thermal noise orients the recovered local moments at random; over 16 realizations, $0.502 \pm 0.004$ of the cells end with a negative $x$ component of the FeCo moment. Among the simulated states, the probe transmission, reflection, and absorption fractions vary by at most 0.02. The magnetic Faraday and Kerr rotations are much more sensitive and become about 12 and 130 times smaller, respectively, in the stochastically recovered state than in a saturated film. The reflected signal also contains a magnetization-independent geometric background, which can be removed by subtracting a reference signal. These results link the switching efficiency to the guided-mode absorption profile and predict polarization-based readout of the simulated magnetic states. The model assumes a homogeneous film and neglects spatial exchange stiffness and subsequent domain coarsening.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Arief Mulyana, Budi Adiperdana, Ayi Bahtiar

item.title: Recovering topological information of light by topological learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.06542v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The evolution of modern-day communication networks towards enhanced capacity and robustness is driving interest in topological light wave as a next-generation information carrier. However, harnessing its potential is hindered by the lack of an effective topological reader, particularly when strong disorder renders conventional readout intractable. Here we address this by introducing TOPO$^{2}$, an artificial intelligence framework that leverages on topological learning to recover topological information from light. We demonstrate it on highly distorted optical fields with embedded Skyrmion topologies, showing that we can extract the topological numbers in a single shot with just a conventional camera. We showcase its capability in a TOPO$^{2}$-based communication scheme, sending and recovering information encoded in a topological alphabet, confirming that it outperforms conventional approaches. Our connection of topological photonics with topological AI as a powerful paradigm for robust high-capacity information encoding and processing opens a new path towards topological information optics.
item.dc:creator: Benquan Wang, Trishita Das, Yuhan Peng, Tatjana Kleine, Shanshan Chang, Jinhui Chen, Nilo Mata-Cervera, Chunyu Li, Kelin Xia, Andrew Forbes, Yijie Shen

item.title: Energy-selective control of noise-assisted multipulsing by weak optical seeding in the dissipative-soliton-resonance regime
item.description: arXiv:2609.30522v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate how weak optical injection changes single-pulse operation in a laser in the dissipative-soliton-resonance regime. The energy scans show that a small injected field suppresses multipulsing and extends predominantly single-pulse operation to higher energies. Further increasing the seed power makes this extended range nonuniform: regions of enhanced multipulse formation alternate with regions of suppression. We analyze timing and optical-phase fluctuations of the injection field. At the lowest energies, these fluctuations cause continuous-wave and multipulse generation to dominate the laser output. At the highest energies, injection-field phase fluctuations promote multiple pulses, whereas time fluctuations suppress them. Deterministic calculations without noise or injection show that both single pulses and prepared pulse pairs can persist under the same settings. We show that the spectral entropy of a dissipative soliton reflects changes in individual pulse spectra and pulse interference. It characterizes the probabilistic transition between single- and multipulse regimes, but it does not, by itself, predict in detail which regime the laser will form. Together, the results connect the energy-selective action of optical injection to pulse formation and structure, while distinguishing persistence of a prepared pulse from its formation out of a background.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir L. Kalashnikov, Alexander Rudenkov, Evgeni Sorokin, Irina T. Sorokina

item.title: Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells
item.description: arXiv:2610.32756v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware and thus trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QPPI), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information, and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. QPPI enables all-optical and label-free studies of contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes. It provides both structural and functional readouts at sufficient frame rates to resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. Conventional fluorescent labels bleach over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring. Instead, QPPI enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast and provides structural readouts similar to those provided by established fluorescent labels, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length. It also offers previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, which provides a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Kreiss Roohian, Nachiket Pathak, David Ripp, Mitchell Harling, Nils M. Kronenberg, Marcel Schubert, Malte C. Gather

item.title: Landscape of scattering universality with general dispersion relations
item.description: arXiv:2509.01782v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Universality in physics describes how disparate systems can exhibit identical low-energy behavior. Here, we reveal a rich landscape of new universal scattering phenomena governed by the interplay between an interaction and a system's density of states. We investigate one-dimensional scattering with dispersion relations $\epsilon(k)=|k|^m$ and $\epsilon(k)=\operatorname{sgn}(k)|k|^m$ for any real $m>1$. For emitter scattering and separable potentials, including contact potentials, we classify the zero-energy $S$-matrix limits. These universal $S$-matrix fixed points depend solely on the dispersion exponent $m$ and a finite set of integers characterizing the low-momentum interaction structure. This classification extends far beyond the standard quadratic-dispersion case ($m=2$). We further derive a generalized Levinson's theorem relating the total winding of the $S$-matrix determinant to the number of bound states. Finally, for contact potentials and analytic monomial dispersions, we analyze the leading low-energy expansion of the scattering phase near these fixed points and extract the corresponding Wigner-delay scaling. Our findings are directly relevant to synthetic quantum systems, where engineered dispersion relations in atomic arrays and photonic crystals offer a platform to explore these universal behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Yidan Wang, Xuesen Na, Michael J. Gullans, Susanne Yelin, Alexey V. Gorshkov

item.title: Advancing optical imaging systems with digital fabrication
item.description: arXiv:2605.00853v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optical imaging technologies are central to discovery in the life and physical sciences, yet their impact depends on how readily they can be built, adapted, and sustained across laboratories. Digital fabrication, including desktop 3D printing, offers new ways to engineer imaging instruments by simplifying assembly, lowering replication barriers, and enabling modular integration and local refinement. Here we examine, using open microscopy as a transparent case, how digitally fabricated components support adaptable, research-grade optical systems while enabling faster innovation cycles and distributed improvement. We outline practical design guidelines and discuss emerging developments that may further advance accessible, high-performance imaging.

item.title: Quantum Imaging via Kurtosis-Difference Weighted Covariance on 2D Camera
item.description: arXiv:2606.31005v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Camera-based quantum imaging detects spatially correlated photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). Conventional covariance methods typically require tens of thousands of frames to extract weak correlations from noise. While thick crystals can increase photon flux, they generate photon pairs from multiple emission positions within the crystal, producing multiple correlation centers with complex pairing geometries. In addition, conventional covariance methods assume a single pre-selected correlation center and cannot fully exploit these distributed correlations. We demonstrate that kurtosis difference, a fourth-order statistic measuring tail similarity, effectively discriminates correlated pixel pairs even when correlation coefficients remain low. Weighting covariance by an exponential function of absolute kurtosis difference can select symmetric pixels while preserving true coincidences. This kurtosis weighting automatically identifies correlated pairs within a broad search region and accommodates multiple pairing geometries without requiring precise correlation center calibration. At 5000 frames, our method yields a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) exceeding 7, whereas standard covariance remains below 2. Compared with standard covariance, the method reduces the acquisition time by 40-fold and could enable practical quantum imaging in sparse correlated-photon regimes.

item.title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
item.description: arXiv:2610.11892v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The extreme intensity of X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses has enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to enable biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Building on improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to ~20 to 30 Angstrom, even though the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.
